prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

The concept was picked up in the United States by the American Planning Association and American Association of Retired Persons, as well as by international advocates including the Bicycle Empowerment Network based in Cape Town and Embarq in Mexico City (Prytherch, 2018). Such terminology according to Zavetoski and Agyeman (2015) denotes a form of “street-level spatial justice,” a “democratization of the street” by decentering drivers and redistributing the right of the right-of-way to the public; and Litman (2015, p. 14) suggests that complete streets policies “help achieve equity objectives by giving non-drivers a fair share of road space.” The concept of complete streets is not without criticism, however: Zavetoski and Agyeman (2015), for instance, propose that such language dehumanizes road users and presumes an unjust rationality to modal choice. Moreover it presumes streets exist in the abstract by isolating the designated area from the other parts of the city. 240 A. WOOD A number of organizations have attempted to codify a set of metrics for assessing walkability: as early as 1997, the U.S. Department of Transportation developed a walkability checklist to allow parents and children to characterize the walkability of their neighborhood (U.S. Department of Transportation, 1997). In 2006, Krambeck (2006) proposed a qualitative analysis of walking condi- tions called the Global Walkability Index that included a public survey. In 2008, the World Bank proposed another five dimensions—accessibility/mobility (i.e., the distance and duration of the average walking trip), safety (i.e., the rate of pedestrian fatalities per population), security (i.e., the rate of pedestrian-targeted crime), legality (i.e., pedestrian laws and rights) and public expenditure (i.e., percent of total urban infrastructure and maintenance funds spent on pedestrian facilities)—to measure the pedestrian environment in cities of the Global South (Montgomery & Roberts, 2008). In 2018, the Institute for Transportation and Development Policy (ITDP), a New York–based sustainable transport advocacy organization introduced “Pedestrians First: A Tool for Walkable Cities,” another tool to enable cities to measure the features that promote walking. This set of 11 indicators considers walkways, crosswalks, visual frontage, physical frontage, shade and connectivity as essential charac- teristics of walkability (ITDP, 2018). These attempts to assess the walkability of an urban area and its associated infrastructure are flawed because these metrics are generally cumbersome to measure. Likewise, where it is possible to measure the walkability of a neighborhood, it is more complicated on a city-scale. Moreover, these indices fail to adequately consider why people walk, focusing too heavily on the characteristics of the pedestrian environment. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups

Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort

- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

WOOD A number of organizations have attempted to codify a set of metrics for assessing walkability: as early as 1997, the U.S. Department of Transportation developed a walkability checklist to allow parents and children to characterize the walkability of their neighborhood (U.S. Department of Transportation, 1997). In 2006, Krambeck (2006) proposed a qualitative analysis of walking condi- tions called the Global Walkability Index that included a public survey. In 2008, the World Bank proposed another five dimensions—accessibility/mobility (i.e., the distance and duration of the average walking trip), safety (i.e., the rate of pedestrian fatalities per population), security (i.e., the rate of pedestrian-targeted crime), legality (i.e., pedestrian laws and rights) and public expenditure (i.e., percent of total urban infrastructure and maintenance funds spent on pedestrian facilities)—to measure the pedestrian environment in cities of the Global South (Montgomery & Roberts, 2008). In 2018, the Institute for Transportation and Development Policy (ITDP), a New York–based sustainable transport advocacy organization introduced “Pedestrians First: A Tool for Walkable Cities,” another tool to enable cities to measure the features that promote walking. This set of 11 indicators considers walkways, crosswalks, visual frontage, physical frontage, shade and connectivity as essential charac- teristics of walkability (ITDP, 2018). These attempts to assess the walkability of an urban area and its associated infrastructure are flawed because these metrics are generally cumbersome to measure. Likewise, where it is possible to measure the walkability of a neighborhood, it is more complicated on a city-scale. Moreover, these indices fail to adequately consider why people walk, focusing too heavily on the characteristics of the pedestrian environment. A clearer conceptualization of walkability is needed to provide the theoretical scaffolding for the remainder of this study.
